comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write to strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety. A $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee would effectively end Optional Practical Training for most international students. That would harm American science, the American economy, and the United States’ standing in the world, without meaningfully serving the rule’s stated goals.

First, the fee does not fit its stated purpose. DHS justifies the rule as a way to strengthen program integrity, but a flat fee of this size applies equally to every student, and the overwhelming majority of OPT participants are doing exactly what the program intends: gaining practical experience in their field at universities, hospitals, laboratories, and companies. DHS already has oversight tools, such as training plans, employer reporting, and site visits, and the rule itself discusses extending these measures more broadly. That approach would strengthen oversight without making OPT unaffordable for the students it exists to serve.

Second, in practice the cost will fall on students. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the fee on to students or employers. $70,000 exceeds the annual stipend of most PhD students in the United States and the first-year salary of many new graduates. Few students could pay it, and few employers will pay it to hire an entry-level graduate. Universities will face the same pressure, so whether a student is recommended for OPT would depend on the institution’s budget rather than the student’s merit. Students at less wealthy institutions would be hurt most.

Third, the rule would undermine practical training as part of education. DHS expects schools to steer students away from pre-completion OPT, because splitting OPT would cost $100,000. Pre-completion OPT is how many students gain internship and research experience while they study. Discouraging it makes American degrees less valuable and less competitive with programs abroad.

Fourth, comparing OPT to H-1B misunderstands the program. OPT is time-limited practical training directly related to a student’s field of study. It is an extension of education, not a substitute for a work visa. Setting fees to “align” with H-1B treats training as a labor loophole and ignores the long-standing recognition that practical experience is part of an education.

Fifth, the rule wastes public investment. Many international graduate students are trained with support from federal research grants, which U.S. taxpayers fund. OPT is often the main way the country gets a return on that investment: graduates apply what they learned in American labs and companies, pay taxes, start businesses, and often stay to fill critical roles. This rule would ensure that federally funded training mostly benefits other countries’ economies.

Sixth, the rule would weaken American leadership in science and technology. The best students choose where to study based partly on post-study work opportunities, and competitor countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia offer post-graduation work pathways without anything like this fee. If OPT becomes unaffordable, top talent will go elsewhere, and so will the research, patents, and companies they produce. The United States has also gained enormous soft power from generations of international students who trained and worked here and went on to become leaders in science, business, and government around the world. Closing that pathway gives up an advantage that cannot easily be regained.

Finally, the rule is unfair to students already enrolled. Current international students made multi-year commitments to American institutions based on a program that has existed for decades. Changing its terms this drastically, mid-degree, breaks faith with them.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it due to high fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations. I support efforts to prevent fraud, but these fees are so high that they would effectively shut many qualified students out of a lawful program.

OPT is not a loophole. It is an established part of the F-1 system, with eligibility rules, school oversight, and government authorization. Students come to the United States legally, pay tuition, complete their degrees, and follow the rules with the understanding that they may apply for practical training in their field. OPT is not guaranteed, but people who meet the requirements should have a fair chance to apply. Making that chance depend on whether a school, student, or employer can come up with $70,000 is not reasonable enforcement.

It also makes little sense from the standpoint of American competitiveness. The U.S. spends years educating talented people from around the world. American employers and research teams then have a chance to benefit from the skills those graduates developed here. Why would we want to train these people and then put up a financial wall just as they are ready to contribute? Other countries are competing for the same talent, and they will be happy to welcome graduates who find the U.S. route too expensive.

Universities would pay a price as well. The chance to gain relevant work experience after graduation is one reason students choose to study in America. If OPT becomes financially unrealistic, some students will choose another country before they ever enroll. That means fewer tuition dollars for U.S. schools and less spending at local businesses. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs in the 2024–25 academic year. This proposal puts part of that value at risk.

What concerns me most is the weak connection between the size of these fees and the stated goal of fighting fraud. The proposed rule says the money would go into the U.S. Treasury and would not be specifically set aside for OPT investigations or enforcement. If the goal is to stop fraudulent employment, why not direct resources toward checking employers, verifying job arrangements, and investigating violations? A $70,000 charge does not tell us whether a job is legitimate. It mainly tells us who can afford to pay.

The burden on smaller institutions is especially troubling. DHS’s own analysis estimates that 98 small institutions could face annual fee costs exceeding 20% of their estimated revenue after the transition period. For some schools, that is money that could otherwise support teaching, student services, and research.

Fraud should be taken seriously. But legitimate students and the schools that educate them should not be priced out of OPT because of wrongdoing by others. I urge DHS to withdraw this fee proposal and pursue targeted, evidence-based enforcement instead.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they harm students and U.S. competitiveness.

The proposal also creates uncertainty for students already years into their degrees. We made substantial educational and personal commitments under an existing framework. A financial barrier introduced near the end of that training could sharply restrict our opportunities after years of work.
I urge DHS to withdraw these proposed fees. At a minimum, DHS should evaluate the effects on academic research, nonprofit institutions, small employers, and currently enrolled students, and consider alternatives that address documented misconduct without making legitimate practical training financially inaccessible.
The United States benefits when people it has helped train can continue contributing to its research and innovation. This proposal risks driving that expertise away.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Joshlin Sheridan
comments.commentText:
As an academic advisor in the Opportunity Program at Skidmore College, I work closely with students from low-income backgrounds, many of whom are interested in pursuing careers in STEM and health-related fields. Through this work, I see how access to higher education can open doors to opportunities that might otherwise be out of reach. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Acron Aviation Academy
comments.commentText:
On behalf of Acron Aviation Academy, an FAA-approved flight training institution that enrolls international students in F-1 status, we respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorizations.
As a flight school that prepares future professional pilots for careers in commercial aviation, we believe the proposed fee structure would have severe unintended consequences for students, educational institutions, and the broader U.S. aviation industry.
OPT is a critical component of aviation training for many international students as this is how pilot graduates build the flight hours necessary to qualify for airline employment. For international students, OPT provides a lawful avenue to gain this practical experience while contributing to the U.S. aviation training ecosystem.
Most importantly, the employment of international student graduates does not reduce opportunities for domestic graduates. Due to normal workforce turnover and continued industry demand, there is a significant and ongoing need for qualified flight instructors. As a Part 141 flight training provider training more than 1,000 students annually, Acron Aviation Academy prioritizes hiring its own graduates because they are already trained in our curriculum, operational procedures, and safety standards. To meet our instructional needs, we depend on both domestic and international graduates. The availability of OPT is therefore critical to maintaining our workforce and ensuring continuity of training operations.
The proposed fee of a minimum of $70,000 per student would effectively eliminate participation for institutions such as Acron Aviation Academy. Flight training organizations typically operate on narrow margins and are unable to absorb costs of this magnitude. While DHS notes that institutions may pass such costs on to students, this is not a realistic solution. Flight training already requires substantial financial investment due to aircraft acquisition, maintenance, fuel, insurance, and operational expenses. Neither schools nor students are positioned to absorb an additional fee of this size.
The practical effect of this proposal would likely be a significant decline in international student enrollment. This would have serious consequences for flight training institutions that rely on international students as an important component of their student population and future instructor workforce. For Acron Aviation Academy, reduced enrollment would directly impact business operations, growth, and sustainability.
Furthermore, the proposed fee would substantially reduce the number of graduates available to serve as flight instructors. Flight instructors are essential to the aviation training pipeline, providing the instruction necessary to prepare future commercial pilots and airline pilots. Restricting access to OPT would weaken the pilot training at a time when the aviation industry continues to require a strong and reliable supply of qualified pilots and instructors.
The proposed fee is extraordinarily high compared to existing immigration-related fees and appears disconnected from the actual administrative costs associated with reviewing and monitoring OPT participants. DHS states that the proposal is intended to combat fraud and protect U.S. workers.
However, imposing a fee of this magnitude on every participating student, regardless of compliance history or field of study, penalizes legitimate educational institutions and law-abiding students rather than targeting specific instances of fraud. Enhanced compliance measures, targeted audits, and improved enforcement would be more effective and less disruptive alternatives.
We respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule or, at minimum, substantially reconsider the proposed fee amounts. If DHS determines that additional program oversight funding is necessary, any fee should be reasonably related to administrative costs and should not create barriers that effectively eliminate participation in OPT.
The proposed fees would impose an unsustainable financial burden on both flight training institutions and international students, effectively limiting access to lawful practical training opportunities. The resulting decline in international student participation would adversely affect flight schools' ability to maintain an adequate instructor workforce and support the aviation training pipeline. Ultimately, the proposal would undermine workforce development and pilot training capacity while providing little evidence that it would meaningfully advance the stated goals of fraud prevention, program integrity, or protection of U.S. workers.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee structure harms students, educational institutions, and the aviation industry.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 RIN
As a concerned citizen, I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing fees of $70,000 for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for any subsequent recommendation for an F-1 nonimmigrant student. As described in the Department of Homeland Security’s notice of proposed rulemaking, the stated objectives include combating fraud, strengthening the integrity of the immigration system, and protecting U.S. workers. However, the proposed fee structure is fundamentally disproportionate to the administrative function it seeks to regulate and fails to adequately account for the practical realities of higher education, international student advising, and the U.S. labor market.
The proposed rule claims that this preposterously massive fees would make up for fewer students applying; however, the reality is that virtually no students would be applying for OPT as students, universities, and employers do not have the amount of money that it takes to recommend even one student for OPT. Additionally, many students do volunteering or unpaid employment that is directly related to their major. This fulfills the requirements of a permissible OPT employer, but no one is going to pay $70,000 for practical training without compensation. USCIS would face a huge financial shortfall without the many OPT applications submitted annually, and the U.S. would lose out on many students using their education to benefit the country without compensation.
With few students applying for OPT, universities and colleges across the nation will see significant decreases in international student enrollment as students around the world will learn that practical training is no longer deemed to be a valuable part of education. A domino effect will ensue. Fewer students means budget deficits, budget deficits will result in cutting of faculty, staff, and resources; cuts to staffing levels and support systems will result in lower quality of education for domestic students. Whether the federal government wants to acknowledge it or not, the success of a high-quality education for its own residents and citizens is dependent upon international students. It would be foolish to ultimately harm a country’s education system as a result of an injudicious governmental decision-making. The claim that students will still want to come for the U.S.’s high caliber education is laughable as without global student mobility and international students, our schools will no longer be held in high esteem. Not only will U.S. institutions of higher education suffer, but so will the labor market. Higher education is designed to fill gaps in the workforce and to prepare graduates for entering the professional sphere. By removing significant numbers of graduates (international students), employers will not be able to fill vacancies with qualified individuals as they will have left the country. Has not competition always proven to make a country stronger?
This proposed rule incorrectly assumes that a student will smoothly go through the process of applying and being approved for OPT without addressing any of the complications that would result from changes to a student’s initial plan or a negative adjudication from USCIS.
If a student has applied for OPT but changes their mind and needs to withdraw their I-765 application, will they get a refund? From whom? In what time frame? Dealing with massive amounts of money does not provide flexibility for cash-strapped institutions, families, or employers. If they then decide to apply in the future, would it be $70,000 or $30,000, since they withdraw their initial recommendation?
If the student applies for OPT but then gets accepted into a new education program and transfers their SEVIS record, do they get a refund?
If the student is denied OPT but then wants to re-apply within the appropriate timeframe, will they need to pay again, or is the initial recommendation fee enough?
This proposed rule, in addition to recent rules, appears to be moving in different directions in terms of what the government believes to be within the scope of a DSO’s responsibilities. In the elimination of D/S rule, responsibility was taken away from the DSOs and given to immigration officers. In a complete contradiction, now, the government believes that DSOs should be career experts of every academic and professional field, responsible for choosing which students are the most eligible to be recommended for OPT. It is not the role of a DSO to determine who is more qualified and which employment is the most valuable. Placing the onus of selecting a handful of students out of thousands also opens universities and DSOs to discrimination lawsuits from disgruntled students who are eligible for OPT but are not seen as worthy of this elephantine fee. How are schools and DSOs supposed to make these decisions and be able to back them up from a legal perspective?
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are disproportionate, unaffordable, and will harm students and the U.S. labor market.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Delaware State University
comments.commentText:
I am writing on behalf of Delaware State University where I serve as the Associate Vice President for Research. Delaware State University is an HBCU and an emerging research institution. We have six doctoral programs in STEM areas and our programs educate largely African-American students, but also a few international students, primarily from Africa (e.g. Nigeria, Cameroon, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire). These students find their way to us largely through connections with family in the U.S. Upon receiving their PhDs all of these students wish to stay in the US to continue working in scientific research, as the infrastructure for research is very limited in their home countries.
If the proposed OPT rule goes into effect it will have a significant negative impact on DSU research. Almost all of the international students who graduate from our PhD programs stay on after graduation under the OPT program and continue to work on their research. This is about 1 student/year. The program is a win for everyone. The graduate is able to build their credentials with additional research publications or learning a new laboratory technique, while the faculty researcher reaps the benefit of their investment in training the graduate. The graduates continue to work on the research when they are at their most productive - after they have received their doctoral level training. The length of the training is usually not long - 9 to 12 months, but it can really advance the research at DSU.
At a cost of $70,000 DSU and its researchers will not be able to afford to keep graduates on for OPT. This will have a significant negative impact on DSU's research enterprise, without providing benefit for anyone else. Graduates on these short-term OPT appointments are not taking away jobs from Americans. As an emerging research institution, faculty at DSU do not have sufficient grant funds to hire a post-doctoral researcher for the 2 - 3 years that these appointments require. A PhD graduate on OPT usually works for only a little more than the stipend or research assistantship they received as a student. They are happy to do that as they build their qualifications and search for more permanent employment. In spite of their short-term nature, the OPT appointments are usually very productive because the graduate already knows the research and the laboratory environment. Eliminating graduates on OPT from the research staff of DSU investigators will reduce the productivity of their research and DSU's overall research enterprise.
On behalf of our researchers at Delaware State University please reconsider this policy.
Thank you,
Melissa A. Harrington, PhD
Associate Vice President for Research
Delaware State University
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT rule will have a significant negative impact on university research.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Shubhang Goswami
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

I am a physics graduate student at University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

This proposal would de-facto prevent the majority of my colleagues and me from advancing U.S. research and economy thus ensuring us to take our expertise, our taxes, and our labor with us to other countries.

Furthermore, International students contributed roughly $43 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 375,000 jobs in a single academic year. Post-graduation work opportunity is a central reason students such as me choose the U.S. over other countries. This ruling would cut tuition revenue that cross-subsidizes domestic students, along with spending on housing, retail, services etc that college towns such as Urbana-Champaign depend on. OPT, and STEM OPT in particular, is the primary bridge through which U.S.-trained graduates in sciences and engineering enter the American workforce. Employers will lose access to these graduates in many STEM specialties where there is already a shortage of domestic workers, thus significantly weakening the United States' competitiveness in emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and quantum computing. In fact, a large portion of US billion dollar ventures have been created by people who were once international students who used this pathway. Thus I urge the DHS to withdraw this ruling.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Shubhang Goswami
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the excessive OPT fees will harm students, the STEM talent pipeline, and the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Larissa Hohl
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for international students seeking employment authorization through Optional Practical Training (OPT).

International students come to the United States through legal channels, comply with strict immigration regulations, and invest significant amounts of their own money in their education. Many pay their entire tuition out of pocket, without access to federal financial aid or other benefits available to domestic students.

After graduation, OPT provides an opportunity for these students to apply their education and skills in the U.S. workforce. When legally authorized to work, international graduates contribute to the economy by filling positions, paying taxes, spending money in their communities, and bringing valuable knowledge and skills to American employers.

A $70,000 fee would create an enormous financial barrier for qualified graduates, many of whom have already made substantial financial investments in their education. It would also discourage talented international graduates from contributing to the U.S. economy and could push employers to seek talent elsewhere.

There is an important contradiction in making it increasingly difficult for people to remain and work in the United States through established legal pathways while simultaneously emphasizing the importance of legal immigration. If the goal is to encourage compliance with immigration laws, policies should make legal pathways accessible and reasonable, not impose financial barriers that make them practically unattainable.

International students are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for a fair opportunity to contribute to the country where we have legally studied, invested our resources, and developed our professional skills.

I respectfully urge the administration to reconsider this proposal and recognize the economic and educational contributions of international students and graduates.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fee creates an enormous financial barrier and harms the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. The proposed rule would close the main path by which U.S.-trained graduates start working here and contribute to the country.

1. By DHS’s own numbers, the costs are huge and the benefits unmeasured (Section VII.A). DHS estimates costs of up to $8.2 billion a year and $35.1 billion over 10 years in its primary estimate. It says lost OPT participation costs about as much as the “net societal benefits” those graduates’ work would have produced. Yet DHS “cannot confidently predict” how far participation will fall, and it describes the rule’s benefits only qualitatively.

2. The fee does not target fraud (Sections IV.A and V.A). DHS’s examples involve shell employers and document sellers. But the fee is “not tied to a specific employer” and falls on all of the roughly 290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants DHS counts each year. Enforcement against the employers involved, through the site visits and prosecutions that produced DHS’s own examples, would address fraud without penalizing every graduate.

3. The rule would push talent and companies out of the United States. In 2024, temporary visa holders earned 61% of U.S. doctorates in computer and information sciences and 54% in engineering (NSF NCSES). Almost one in four U.S. billion-dollar startups has a founder who first came here as an international student (NFAP, 2026). At $70,000 to $100,000 per student, few schools will pay, and these graduates will build their careers and companies in competing countries.

I urge that DHS withdraw this proposal. At minimum, a final rule should target enforcement at fraudulent employers instead of charging every student, and exempt everyone enrolled before it takes effect.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous

comments.commentText:
RE: Comments on Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees
Agency: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Department of Homeland Security
Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100-0001

To Whom It May Concern,
As a faculty member at Drew University Theological School, I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to establish a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal in its entirety.

Drew University Theological School is an institution committed to academic excellence and innovative research, and this proposed rule introduces catastrophic financial and administrative burdens. Requiring SEVP-certified schools to remit up to $100,000 per student fundamentally misinterprets the fiscal realities of higher education. Higher education institutions cannot absorb these massive costs which means the financial burden will inevitably fall upon the shoulders of students or severely restrict our ability to offer experiential learning opportunities.

In theological education, professional development and vocational formation extend beyond the classroom. Many of the academic programs offered in the Drew University Theological School require supervised internships for our students to engage in experiential learning. Optional Practical Training provides an indispensable extension of this mission, enabling students who bring gifts and expertise from a range of perspectives to apply their academic training in real-world U.S. environments. International graduates contribute to the vitality of congregations and the well-being of communities, including rural and underserved areas where qualified pastoral leadership can be difficult to secure. The proposed fee structure would dismantle this pathway and weaken our regional and national pool of qualified religious professionals.

While I certainly support efforts to protect the integrity of the student visa system, punitive financial barriers targeting legitimate academic programs are a disproportionate and ineffective mechanism to address bad actors. I respectfully ask that DHS withdraw this harmful rule.

Sincerely,

Stephen D. Moore
Edmund S. Janes Professor of New Testament Studies
The Theological School, Drew University

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international undergraduate student studying a STEM field at a university in the United States, and I strongly oppose the proposed rule that would require universities to pay $70,000 for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions.

For students like me, coming to the United States for college is a huge commitment. We spend years working toward this opportunity, and our families often make significant financial sacrifices to support our education. We pay tuition, work hard in our classes, and do everything we can to build a future for ourselves. At the same time, we have to carefully follow immigration rules, maintain our legal status, and make sure we meet every academic and employment requirement.

One of the main reasons many international students choose to study in the United States is the opportunity to gain real-world experience in the field they have spent years studying. As a STEM student, I know that what we learn in the classroom is only part of our education. Being able to apply that knowledge in a professional environment is extremely important, especially in fields like engineering and computer science.

What concerns me most about this proposal is how unrealistic these fees are. Even though the rule would technically require universities to pay them, students would still be the ones affected. Most universities cannot reasonably be expected to pay $70,000 for every international student who wants to participate in OPT. They may pass these costs on to students or stop offering OPT recommendations altogether. Either way, students who have worked hard, followed the rules, and earned their degrees could lose opportunities simply because of money.

I am especially worried about students who are already studying in the United States. When we made the decision to come here, we did so with an understanding of the opportunities available to us, including the possibility of applying for OPT after graduation. We made major financial and personal decisions based on that understanding. While we know OPT is not guaranteed, introducing such a massive financial barrier after students have already invested years into their education feels deeply unfair.

I understand that DHS has a responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers, and I fully support efforts to make sure the system is being used properly. However, I do not see how charging universities tens of thousands of dollars for an OPT recommendation directly addresses those concerns. Students who follow the law should not be treated the same as those who abuse the system.

There are better ways to address fraud, such as stronger verification processes, more oversight of employers, and stricter enforcement against actual violations. These approaches would focus on the problems DHS is trying to solve without making it nearly impossible for legitimate students to gain practical experience.

I also think it is important to recognize what international students contribute to the United States. We support American universities and local businesses, participate in research, and bring different perspectives and skills into classrooms and workplaces. Many of us genuinely want to use what we have learned to contribute to the American economy. Making OPT financially inaccessible could discourage future students from choosing American universities in the first place.

I am not asking for special treatment, and I understand that studying in the United States does not guarantee me a job. All I am asking for is a fair chance to use the education I have worked so hard for. I believe those opportunities should depend on our qualifications, hard work, and willingness to follow the rules, not on whether a university can afford an unreasonable fee.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw this proposed fee structure. Protecting the integrity of the immigration system is important, but it should not come at the expense of students who have done everything expected of them.

For many of us, this is not just a policy change or a financial issue. It affects years of planning, our families’ sacrifices, and the futures we have been working toward since we decided to pursue an education in the United States.

Thank you for taking the time to consider how this proposal would affect international students like me.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100 – Optional Practical Training Fees

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed Optional Practical Training fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation.

I am an international student from Germany who graduated from Lourdes University in Ohio with a Bachelor's degree in Psychology. Throughout my education, I worked hard academically, participated in collegiate athletics, and contributed to my university community.

After graduating, I received authorization through Optional Practical Training and began working as an Employment Services Coordinator at a nonprofit organization that supports refugees and newcomers in the United States.

Through my employment, I help individuals find jobs, develop professional skills, and become financially independent. OPT has allowed me to apply my American education in a meaningful professional setting while contributing to the community that welcomed me.

The proposed fees would create an extraordinary financial barrier for future international students. A $70,000 fee is far beyond what most recent graduates could reasonably afford, and many universities and nonprofit employers would also struggle to cover such an expense.

For students pursuing careers in psychology, social services, education, and other community-oriented fields, the proposed fees could make practical training effectively inaccessible.

I also believe the proposal could discourage talented international students from choosing American universities. Many students invest significant financial resources into obtaining a U.S. education with the understanding that they may have an opportunity to gain relevant professional experience afterward.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider these proposed fees and evaluate less financially burdensome alternatives that would address legitimate concerns about program integrity without preventing qualified graduates from participating in practical training.

In the long term, I believe the United States risks losing not only the cultural diversity that international students bring, but also talented, highly educated, and motivated individuals who have the potential to make meaningful contributions to this country. International graduates bring unique perspectives, valuable skills, and a strong willingness to contribute to American society. By creating significant financial barriers to practical training opportunities, the United States could discourage future generations of talented students from pursuing their education and careers here. Ultimately, I believe this would represent a loss not only for international students themselves, but also for American employers, local communities, and the country's long-term economic and social well-being.

Thank you for considering my perspective.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public Comment: Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 | RIN 1653-AB01
I oppose DHS’s proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. The proposed OPT 1-year post-graduation work authorization pathway to further our training would become 149x more expensive than today. This proposal is disproportionate, poorly targeted, and risks restricting legitimate training while imposing unsustainable costs on students, institutions, and employers.
1. U.S. Workforce Capacity and Healthcare Access
The rule ignores critical healthcare workforce needs. The Commonwealth Fund reports that 43 million Americans live in rural areas with primary-care shortages, projecting that rural physician supply will meet just 68% of demand by 2037. Hospitals also face severe shortages of pharmacists, laboratory scientists, and imaging professionals. As a cancer research PhD and healthcare professional, I know OPT graduates in biomedical and health fields contribute significantly to clinical operations, research, and patient care. This fee narrows this vital talent pool without ensuring vacant positions are filled by U.S. workers. F-1 OPT/STEM OPT students do not have an open employment authorization document (EAD) to work anywhere. Every single job must be directly related to their major field of study. For the 24-month STEM OPT extension, the Form I-983 attestation is a safeguard against replacing existing domestic labor.
2. Economic Consequences for American Institutions
International students drive economic growth. NAFSA estimates they contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024–25. With U.S. healthcare spending at an OECD-highest 17.2% of GDP in 2024, workforce capacity and research innovation are vital. DHS must assess the severe downstream impacts on enrollment, research recruitment, and local economies rather than assuming reduced OPT numbers automatically benefit domestic workers.
3. The Fee Does Not Address or Prevent Fraud
DHS identifies valid concerns like fictitious employers and false records, but levying an exorbitant fee on schools does not address them. It fails to verify that employment exists or relates to a student's major. In reality, F-1 students already undergo intense institutional oversight. To maintain status, they complete coursework mapped to Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) and must regularly submit mandatory, structured employer evaluations to their Designated School Official (DSO). Under 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(10)–(11) and Wash. Alliance of Tech. Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), OPT is legally validated as limited training related to a student’s course of study. Enforcement should build on this framework, not create arbitrary financial walls.
4. Correcting Misconceptions on Tax Treatment and Equity
Commenters argue F-1 students hold a hiring advantage due to FICA exemptions. Per the IRS, certain nonresident F-1 students are exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes on authorized employment for their first five calendar years. However, they still pay full federal, state, and local income taxes. Crucially, they pay into these systems while being entirely excluded from the benefits they fund, including Federal Pell Grants, federal loans, Federal Work-Study, and ACA subsidies. They are also barred from incentive programs like Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), which forgives debt for U.S. citizens after 120 qualifying payments. Given that international students pay significantly higher tuition alongside steep SEVIS and visa fees that fund immigration worker jobs, the claim of a competitive advantage is groundless.
5. Fee Pass-Through and Institutional Burdens
DHS acknowledges schools may pass this fee to students or employers. A $70,000 or $30,000 fee would price out qualified talent, compounding existing tuition disparities. If schools absorb it, they will reduce student services or scale back vital academic programs. Furthermore, the 60-day implementation timeline completely disregards reliance interests. Students have committed tuition and structured their careers around the current framework. DHS must provide at least a 2-year transition window to protect current students.
6. Requested Action and Targeted Alternatives
DHS should withdraw this proposal and prioritize risk-based employer audits, worksite verifications, and penalties for confirmed violators. SEVIS data should prompt targeted investigations rather than justifying blanket fees.
As a lawful academic immigrant with a PhD in biomedical research, I contribute through skilled work, tuition, and taxes. I also volunteer with the American Red Cross, Reading Partners, senior care initiatives, and kids with disabilities.

I support strict oversight, but urge DHS to implement an evidence-based, proportionate policy that targets fraud directly without harming lawful students, universities, and the U.S. healthcare system.

Thank you for your consideration.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they impose unsustainable costs and harm the healthcare workforce.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing as an F-1 international student attending a public university in the United States to express my concerns regarding the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

I understand that DHS wants to prevent fraud, protect American workers, and ensure that the OPT program is being used appropriately. I believe these are important goals. However, I am concerned that the proposed fees would prevent many legitimate international students from gaining practical experience after completing their education in the United States.

Like many international students, I chose to pursue higher education in the United States because of its academic opportunities and the ability to apply classroom knowledge in a professional environment. International students invest significant amounts of time, money, and effort into earning their degrees. Practical training provides an important opportunity to develop professional skills and gain experience related to their education.

OPT is an important part of that educational experience. Students spend years studying, paying tuition, following immigration regulations, and preparing to enter their professional fields. For many of us, OPT provides an opportunity to apply those skills after graduation.

My primary concern is that the proposed fees would create a financial barrier unrelated to a student's qualifications, compliance with immigration rules, or ability to contribute professionally.

Although the proposed rule places the payment responsibility on universities, a $70,000 fee for each student's initial OPT recommendation would be an enormous financial commitment. Many universities, particularly public institutions with limited budgets, may be unable to pay such fees. As a result, students could lose access to OPT even if they have followed every immigration requirement and secured legitimate employment opportunities.

I am also concerned about the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions. Students in STEM fields often benefit from additional professional training to develop specialized skills. Requiring institutions to pay as much as $100,000 across initial OPT and a subsequent extension could discourage participation in these opportunities.

I respectfully ask DHS to consider how these fees could affect students who are already enrolled, universities that cannot afford the payments, and employers offering legitimate training opportunities.

I recognize the importance of preventing fraud within the OPT program, but I believe stronger compliance monitoring, targeted investigations, improved employer verification, and more reasonable administrative fees could address those concerns without creating such substantial barriers for students who follow the rules.

I also ask DHS to consider the expectations of students who enrolled in American universities under the existing OPT framework. International students make significant financial, academic, and personal commitments based on the opportunities available when they begin their degrees. A sudden change of this magnitude could substantially alter their ability to complete their educational and professional plans.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees and evaluate less burdensome alternatives that maintain program integrity while preserving access to legitimate practical training.

International students come to the United States to learn, gain experience, and contribute their knowledge and skills. I hope DHS will consider the impact this proposal could have on students who have worked hard to pursue their education and careers responsibly.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

An International Student

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security,

I would like to raise a concern that seems to be missing from much of the discussion surrounding the proposed OPT fees: What happens to the jobs that the United States already struggles to fill?

There is a significant difference between protecting American workers from unfair competition and preventing qualified people from filling positions where workers are genuinely needed.

Education is one example. The United States has faced teacher shortages for years, particularly in special education, where recruiting and retaining qualified professionals remains a challenge. According to an analysis of state-reported teacher shortage data, 45 states identified special education as a shortage area during the 2024–2025 school year.

These shortages exist for reasons. Teaching can be demanding, salaries are not always competitive, and special education often requires additional training, patience, and professional responsibility. Not everyone wants to enter these fields, and many who do eventually decide to leave.

There is nothing wrong with Americans choosing other careers or seeking better opportunities. Everyone should have that freedom. But when schools cannot find enough qualified professionals, why should the government also make it harder for qualified international graduates who are willing to do this work?

The United States already recognizes the importance of attracting people into education. Federal programs such as Teacher Loan Forgiveness provide financial incentives for eligible teachers, including those working in special education. These programs reflect an understanding that teaching is essential and that certain positions can be difficult to fill.

It seems contradictory to recognize the need for more educators through one set of policies while introducing financial barriers that could prevent internationally educated professionals from entering the same workforce through lawful practical training.

I understand concerns about protecting employment opportunities for American citizens. American workers deserve fair wages, reasonable working conditions, and access to good jobs. However, protecting workers should not mean keeping necessary positions unfilled.

If an American citizen is qualified and willing to take a position, that person deserves fair consideration. But if a school has struggled to recruit qualified staff, preventing an eligible international graduate from working does not automatically create another qualified American applicant.

It may simply leave the position vacant.

And in education, a vacant position is not just an employment statistic. It can mean students receiving less individual attention, teachers carrying heavier workloads, and children with disabilities waiting longer for the support they need.

I also believe we should question whether extremely high OPT fees would address the actual reasons behind workforce shortages. They would not improve teacher salaries, reduce workloads, or make difficult positions more attractive to American workers. Instead, they could remove another source of qualified applicants without solving the underlying problems.

International graduates should still be required to meet professional licensing standards, employment requirements, and immigration regulations. No one should receive a job simply because they are willing to take it. But people who are properly trained, qualified, and legally authorized should have a fair opportunity to contribute.

A country should not have to choose between protecting its own workers and allowing qualified international graduates to fill genuine workforce needs. These goals can coexist.

I ask DHS to consider the consequences of this proposal for education and other shortage occupations. If the government believes certain jobs should be filled by more American workers, it should invest in making those careers more attractive and accessible. That is a meaningful solution to workforce shortages.

Making it prohibitively expensive for international graduates to participate in lawful practical training is not a substitute for improving working conditions or addressing recruitment challenges.

It is difficult to justify leaving important work undone while simultaneously discouraging qualified people who are ready and willing to do it.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed OPT fees and adopt policies that protect American workers without unnecessarily restricting access to qualified professionals in fields where they are needed.

Thank you for considering this perspective.
comments.reason: Argues the proposed OPT fees harm critical workforce shortages in areas like special education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing substantial fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). I believe this proposal would create unnecessary financial barriers, discourage talented international students from pursuing education and professional opportunities in the United States, and ultimately undermine the country's economic competitiveness, scientific advancement, and ability to attract and retain skilled professionals.

The United States has long benefited from attracting talented individuals from around the world. International students contribute not only through tuition and living expenses but also through academic research, technological development, entrepreneurship, and participation in the American workforce. Many spend years developing specialized knowledge and skills at American universities, often contributing to research projects that benefit American institutions, industries, and society.

OPT provides an important opportunity for these individuals to apply their education and contribute their expertise within the United States. Imposing fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent participation would make this opportunity financially inaccessible to many qualified individuals and institutions. Rather than evaluating students based on their education, qualifications, and potential contributions, this proposal risks making access to practical training dependent primarily on financial resources.

I am particularly concerned about the long-term consequences for America's scientific and technical workforce. Research and innovation depend on collaboration among individuals with diverse expertise and backgrounds. International graduates contribute to fields such as engineering, biotechnology, healthcare, and emerging technologies. Discouraging these individuals from remaining in the United States to gain professional experience could result in the loss of valuable expertise and research potential. Other countries may benefit from talent that American universities have helped educate and train.

The economic implications also deserve serious consideration. According to the Institute of International Education's Open Doors 2025 report, approximately 294,253 international students participated in OPT during the 2024–2025 academic year. NAFSA estimates that international students collectively contributed approximately $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 American jobs during that academic year. Although these figures do not measure OPT's impact independently, they demonstrate the substantial economic importance of international education.

Furthermore, I question whether imposing such extraordinary fees is an effective or proportionate response to concerns about fraud and program integrity. Preventing fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives. However, financial barriers do not necessarily distinguish legitimate participants from those engaging in misconduct. A policy that broadly penalizes qualified students and institutions risks causing substantial economic and educational harm without adequately addressing the underlying problems.

The proposed fees could also create unintended consequences for American universities and employers. Institutions with limited financial resources may be unable to support OPT participation, while employers could lose access to graduates with specialized skills. Students who have already invested significant time and resources in American education may find that the professional opportunities they reasonably anticipated are no longer financially attainable. Such uncertainty could discourage future international enrollment and weaken the global competitiveness of American higher education.

I respectfully recommend that DHS withdraw the proposed OPT fee structure and instead pursue targeted, evidence-based measures to address documented instances of fraud, including improved employer verification, stronger oversight, and enforcement against individuals or organizations that violate existing regulations. These approaches would more directly address program integrity concerns without imposing excessive financial burdens on legitimate participants.

Before advancing any comparable proposal, DHS should also provide a comprehensive assessment of its potential effects on international student enrollment, university research, workforce availability, economic activity, and America's long-term competitiveness.

The United States should pursue policies that protect its interests while continuing to attract and retain individuals who contribute to its scientific, technological, and economic development. Making practical training financially inaccessible risks achieving the opposite.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw this proposal

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to focus on a question the proposal never answers: why $70,000?

A fee is supposed to bear some relationship to a cost. DHS has published no study tying $70,000 to the expense of processing an OPT recommendation — because no such study could exist. The recommendation itself is a Designated School Official's verification in SEVIS, an administrative act that takes minutes. The government then adjudicates the student's employment authorization for roughly $500. At many public universities, $70,000 exceeds an entire year of in-state tuition. It is not a price derived from a ledger; it is a number chosen because it is high enough to stop the behavior it attaches to.

That is the heart of the problem. A rule that ends a program must be defended as ending a program, with reasons, evidence, and consideration of alternatives. DHS has done none of that here. The proposal contains no serious analysis of alternatives that would achieve its stated goals at lower cost: a tiered fee scaled to school size, a cap on recommendations per institution, a phased rollout that lets schools plan, or — most obviously — targeted enforcement against the bad actors the agency says it is worried about. An agency that skips the alternatives analysis and jumps straight to a price no school can pay has not regulated; it has abolished by arithmetic.

The administrative law problem is not abstract. Courts ask whether an agency examined the relevant data and articulated a satisfactory explanation for its action, including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made. Here the facts DHS found — that some schools would "simply stop recommending OPT" — point in the opposite direction from the choice it made. An agency that concedes its fee will shut down the program it is supposedly administering owes the public an explanation for the shutdown, not a fee schedule.

If OPT should end, Congress can end it, in the open, after debate. If OPT should be reformed, DHS can propose reforms proportionate to real problems, with numbers grounded in real costs. A six-figure fee with no cost basis and no alternatives analysis is neither. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Julie Martin
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. Protecting program integrity and American workers are legitimate objectives, but this proposal lacks adequate evidence that its extraordinary fees will achieve those goals without imposing substantial harm on U.S. universities, employers, and the research enterprise.

1. Insufficient evidence of effectiveness (Section IV)

DHS identifies real instances of OPT fraud, which warrant enforcement. Yet these cases do not establish the prevalence of confirmed fraud across all OPT participants or show that universal fees would prevent it. The proposal does not estimate how many fraudulent applications the fees would deter relative to how many legitimate applicants would lose access. A reduction in overall participation is not evidence of effective fraud detection. DHS should quantify the expected anti-fraud effects and explain the causal basis for its assumptions.

2. Unjustified fee amounts (Section IV.C)

DHS partly justifies the fees by reference to H-1B-related costs and international students' educational expenses. Neither comparison establishes why $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary or proportionate for OPT. The proposal offers no persuasive analysis showing that substantially lower amounts would be ineffective. Moreover, the revenues would enter the U.S. Treasury rather than be directly retained by ICE for enforcement. DHS should provide an evidence-based justification for each fee and distinguish its asserted deterrent effect from actual investments in oversight.

3. Weaknesses in the economic analysis (Section VII.A)

DHS acknowledges uncertainty about how institutions will respond but uses a primary participation estimate based on the average of two assumed scenarios. The low-participation scenario largely excludes students ineligible for STEM OPT extensions while assuming continued support for eligible students. Other plausible outcomes, including widespread reductions in STEM OPT recommendations, are insufficiently examined. The midpoint of two assumptions is not necessarily a reliable prediction.

DHS also uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the opportunity costs of lost participation. A government fee is not an empirical measure of the value of research, work experience, employer productivity, or future innovation. The analysis needs broader sensitivity testing, institution-specific behavioral scenarios, and independent estimates of forgone economic activity.

4. Harm to legitimate participation and U.S. institutions (Sections IV.C and VII.B)

An institution's ability to pay does not reliably indicate whether a student's OPT opportunity is legitimate. Financially constrained universities may be unable to support qualified graduates, while access to funding does not guarantee compliance. DHS explicitly allows schools to shift costs to students or employers, potentially extending the burden beyond their own budgets.

DHS's analysis estimates that 841 of 1,389 small affected institutions could face first-year impacts exceeding 1% of estimated annual revenue, including 116 facing impacts above 20%. Institutions unable to pay may cease recommending OPT altogether. The consequences for U.S. research continuity, recruitment, innovation, and international enrollment deserve fuller examination. Protecting American workers also requires evidence about actual wage and employment effects, rather than assumptions that every lost OPT position will benefit a domestic worker.

5. Better-targeted alternatives (Sections IV.C and VII.B)

DHS discusses enhanced site visits and reporting but dismisses them primarily because they would impose greater administrative demands on government. That is not a sufficient comparison of total costs and benefits. Risk-based employer audits, verification of worksites, improved use of SEVIS data, and stronger penalties for confirmed fraud could focus enforcement on documented vulnerabilities. DHS should compare these approaches against universal fees in terms of fraud reduction, economic costs, and effects on lawful participants.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, substantiate the specific fee levels and expected fraud reduction, revise its economic analysis, and evaluate targeted alternatives. American competitiveness depends on both credible immigration enforcement and a strong educational and scientific workforce. A policy with consequences of this magnitude requires a stronger evidentiary foundation.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they lack evidence and harm universities and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training Fees
As a member of the Council of University Directors of Clinical Psychology (CUDCP), I oppose the proposed
$70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and the additional $30,000
fee for subsequent participation. CUDCP represents over 180 programs who provide doctoral
education in clinical psychology.
Clinical psychology requires extensive specialized training, often including a one-year
postdoctoral fellowship following doctoral education in many states, to prepare highly skilled
psychologists to enter the U.S. workforce. OPT is the key mechanism through which
international trainees can complete these required fellowships, and the proposed fees would
severely restrict access by imposing substantial financial burdens on CUDCP member programs’
universities, with the costs likely passed on to students or fellowship sites. This could
potentially lead programs to eliminate fellowship positions or exclude otherwise qualified
candidates, leading to even more imbalance in provider supply and demand than already exists.
Current research (Cicero et al., 2025) indicates that behavioral health care resources are in
decline, while demands for services are increasing. This mismatch will reach a peak by 2037,
when projected resources will be able to meet only 55% of anticipated demand.
Negative consequences of the proposed rule extend beyond individual trainees. International
professionals contribute to the U.S. workforce through clinical care and research, bringing
valuable scientific expertise related to psychological functioning that strengthens the quality of
psychological services, research, and patient care. Restricting access to specialized training
could further undermine already constrained workforce development and limit the availability
of clinical researchers equipped to advance the field and serve the needs of the U.S. population.
We urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide transparent justification for the
amounts, and explore less burdensome alternatives that preserve appropriate oversight
without creating prohibitive financial barriers to professional training.

Why does this proposal actually matter to the mission of CUDCP and our trainees?
OPT is the primary mechanism through which international trainees obtain authorization to
complete advanced training in the U.S. and is required for specialties such as
neuropsychology. The proposed rule would create a major systemic barrier to completing this
required training, as many programs would be unable to absorb the proposed fees and there
may not be an alternative visa pathway available to these trainees.
If the proposal is finalized, CUDCP member programs’ universities with international trainees
who match with programs through OPT would face the $70,000 fee, with the costs likely
passed on to students or fellowship sites. Of note, employers do not currently pay a fee for
OPT participation! An alternative is H1B/J1 sponsorship, but this is not a viable option for many
fellowship programs. Preliminary work conducted by the Asian Neuropsychology Association
suggests that during the most recent application cycle, only ~35% of fellowship programs
accepted international trainees and either had a known visa mechanism in place or indicated
that some form of sponsorship might be possible but not guaranteed. So, international trainees
already face significant barriers under the current system, and this proposal would compound
these existing visa-related barriers, likely leaving trainees without a viable pathway to
complete our field's required training in the U.S.

Thank you for considering these comments.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees because they impose a financial burden and harm clinical psychology training programs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees (Proposed Rule)

I am an F-1 graduate of Texas A&M University, currently on a STEM OPT extension. I began post-completion OPT in 2024 and now work in data science in the finance industry. I am writing in my personal capacity about the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT.

My concern is the size of the fee relative to what OPT is. OPT is a short, time-limited period of practical training that follows a completed U.S. degree. A fee of $70,000 is larger than the first-year salary in many data science and research roles that recent graduates actually obtain, and it bears no relationship to the administrative cost of a school recommending OPT, or to any individual risk posed by a graduate who has completed a degree and is complying with all reporting requirements.

Because the fee is charged to the school before it may recommend OPT, I am concerned that in practice it will not be absorbed by institutions. Schools will either pass the cost to students or limit their willingness to recommend OPT. Either outcome would effectively make OPT available only to graduates with substantial personal wealth, rather than on the basis of academic completion and a qualifying job — which is what the program is for.

The treatment of "subsequent OPT" affects me directly. I am currently on a STEM OPT extension that was recommended by my school and approved under rules that contained no such fee, and my employer and I arranged my employment in reliance on those rules. The proposal does not make clear whether a STEM OPT extension counts as a subsequent OPT subject to the $30,000 fee, or how any such fee would apply to extensions already in progress. Current participants should not face a five-figure charge, or the threat of one, in the middle of an authorization that was granted under different terms.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee schedule, or, at a minimum, substantially reduce the amounts, tie any fee to actual processing costs, exclude extensions and other OPT periods already authorized, and clarify how the rule would apply to students and graduates already in the OPT pipeline.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Respectfully submitted,
A Texas A&M University graduate on STEM OPT

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Homeland Security Department / U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees (Document 2026-20660 / Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). As an F-1 graduate student currently conducting advanced research in STEM at a U.S. university , I believe this proposal is economically unviable, legally flawed, and severely detrimental to the competitive edge of American higher education and technology sectors.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule based on the following substantive grounds:

1. Arbitrary and Capricious Fee Assessment Beyond Statutory Authority
Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act (IOAA, 31 U.S.C. 9701) and relevant immigration statutes, user fees imposed by federal agencies must be reasonably related to the actual cost of providing a specific service or administrative processing. The proposed imposition of exorbitant fees ($70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent/STEM OPT) far exceeds any legitimate cost-recovery mechanism for SEVP or USCIS administrative oversight. Imposing fees of this magnitude is functionally punitive rather than compensatory, rendering the rule arbitrary, capricious, and an abuse of agency discretion under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA, 5 U.S.C. § 706).

2. Severe Economic Disruption to U.S. Universities and Employers
Shifting such massive financial burdens onto SEVP-certified institutions or F-1 students will have unintended, disastrous consequences for the U.S. economy:
- Financial Strain on Institutions: Universities cannot absorb these fees without drastically raising tuition for all students or cutting research budgets, directly undermining public higher education.
- Loss of U.S. STEM Competitiveness: High-skilled international graduates are vital to U.S. R&D, artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, and biomedical innovation. Exorbitant fees effectively shut out top global talent, forcing critical research and employment to shift overseas to competing nations like Canada, Europe, and Asia.
- Small Business and Startup Harm: Employers who rely on OPT talent—especially mid-sized enterprises and early-stage tech startups—will be unable to subsidize these exorbitant fees or compensate for lost talent pools.

3. Disproportionate Impact on International Students and Equity
F-1 students already contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy while paying full tuition and living expenses without access to federal financial aid. Requiring students or institutions to pay tens of thousands of dollars just to receive temporary hands-on practical training directly linked to their degree renders OPT inaccessible to all but the wealthiest individuals, violating basic principles of educational access and equity.

4. Unsubstantiated Justification Regarding Integrity and Fraud
While program integrity is an essential goal, DHS has failed to provide empirical evidence demonstrating that imposing punitive financial barriers on schools or students is a targeted or effective method for preventing fraud. The existing regulatory frameworks (including SEVIS tracking, Form I-983 training plans for STEM OPT, and institutional reporting) already provide robust oversight. Enhancing compliance should be achieved through streamlined administrative audits, not by pricing legitimate international scholars out of practical training.

Conclusion
The proposed OPT fees will inflict irreparable harm on American universities, damage U.S. economic competitiveness, and unfairly burden global scholars who contribute significantly to the United States.

I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to rescind this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they are economically unviable and legally flawed.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by AAMC
comments.commentText:
The AAMC welcomes the opportunity to comment on the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule: Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees. The introduction of a new fee of $70,000 for initial OPT per F–1 nonimmigrant student, and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT would have a negative impact on the biomedical research workforce, the advancement of biomedical research, and ultimately the health of the American public. We strongly urge DHS to not finalize this proposed rule.

International visa holders contribute to the biomedical research workforce
International visa holders make up a significant portion of biomedical research learners in the United States (U.S.). National Science Foundation (NSF) data show that in 2023, 24% of research doctorate (PhD) recipients and 59% of postdoctoral scholars in the biological and biomedical sciences were temporary visa holders. Many international biomedical PhD students use the F-1 visa mechanism and the majority subsequently participate in Optional Practical Training (OPT) to further their training as a postdoctoral scholar or to get some employment experience. Participating schools must be certified by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP). All AAMC-member institutions utilize SEVP and are eligible to have students engage in OPT. Therefore, many international biomedical graduate students would be impacted by the proposed OPT fee.

As we have stated in previous comments to DHS, for decades, the U.S. has attracted talented international students and postdoctoral scholars to train in our biomedical research facilities; the proposed policy will further deter international PhD students from training in the U.S. International scholars contribute to the intellectual and cultural vibrancy and scientific preeminence of the U.S. biomedical research enterprise. Losing international talent would also lead to a reduction in U.S. competitiveness. Most scientists who are international visa holders remain in the U.S. after their training and contribute to our goal of improving health through discovery.

The fee will lead to increased costs, including loss of investment
The proposed rule states that “DHS believes that the OPT fees are on par with the educational costs that foreign students incur for one or two years of education in a program of study in the U.S.” However, unlike most undergraduate and master’s students, who pay tuition, most biomedical PhD students receive waived tuition and are paid a stipend. This is because biomedical PhD students serve a dual role as trainee and researcher which improves the health of the American people. Most academic institutions do not have the financial resources to cover this proposed fee. They also may not be the employer of those on OPT. Should the new fees be passed on to the students, as allowed in the proposed rule, it would severely limit the number of students who could afford to participate in the OPT program.

In addition to the fee itself, the proposed rule will lead to other financial costs for the institution as they will need to comply with the new rule and adapt their processes for selecting students to recommend for OPT and establish new processes for funding the new fees. To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:

I am an international student, and I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT. Those skills will matter wherever I build my career, including if I return to my home country.

Under Section V.A, schools would have to pay before recommending a student for OPT. Putting the payment obligation on the school still leaves students exposed. If my university asks me to cover the fee, I would face an enormous new expense before earning anything through OPT. If my university cannot afford to pay, I could lose access to training even if I meet the eligibility requirements. And if access depends on finding an employer willing to cover the cost, I could lose opportunities with employers that can offer good training but cannot absorb a fee of that size. For students already enrolled, that uncertainty arrives while we are still paying for our degrees and trying to focus on finishing them.

I take DHS’s concerns about fraud and worker protection seriously. A school’s ability to pay $70,000 tells DHS little about whether a placement is genuine, whether the work relates to the student’s degree, or whether the employer follows applicable labor rules. Section IV.C also explains that the fees would go to the U.S. Treasury. The payments themselves would provide no dedicated funding for the oversight DHS says the program needs. I ask DHS to address the conduct it has identified through targeted employer verification, reviews of suspicious placements, and enforcement where there is evidence of abuse.

DHS’s own regulatory analysis recognizes that the fees could reduce OPT participation. Before adopting any policy that would restrict access this sharply, DHS should assess how many eligible students would lose legitimate training opportunities because their schools, employers, or families cannot pay. It should also account for students who have already committed to tuition and years of study under the existing rules. I urge DHS to withdraw both proposed fees and preserve meaningful access to practical training for students who follow the rules.
